title: Genesis 2. The Cup at Rest.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 2. The Cup at Rest.
God finishes.
He rests.
The seventh day.
Not because He is tired, because the work is complete.
The Cup that was filled across six days of speaking and filling and naming and blessing is now full,
and the hand that filled it lets it sit.
He blesses the day and makes it holy.
Rest is not recovery.
Rest is what fullness looks like when nothing more needs to be added.
Then the lens turns.
The creation account that moved like a river across the heavens and the earth now narrows to one place,
one man, one breath.
No plant was yet in the field.
No rain had fallen.
No man was there to work the ground.
A mist rose from the earth and watered its surface.
And God formed man, dust from the ground, shaped by hands.
Then He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life,
and man became a living soul.
The vessel is dust receiving breath.
The LORD God forms the man from the ground,
breathes the breath of life into his nostrils,
and the man becomes a living soul.
The Cup that received light and water and vegetation now receives something it had not held before:
a living creature formed from the same ground and made alive by God's breath.
God plants a garden in Eden, eastward, and places the man there.
Every tree grows, pleasant to see, good for food.
The tree of life stands in the midst of the garden,
and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is named beside it in the text.
The Cup holds both possibilities from the beginning:
life and the knowledge that can end it.
A river flows out to water the garden and divides into four,
the garden is not closed.
It is watered, it flows outward, it is abundant.
God places the man in the garden to work it and keep it.
He gives a command inside the abundance: eat from every tree, freely,
all of it.
But not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
In the day you eat of it, you will surely die.
The boundary is set inside the abundance, not outside it.
The Cup is not restricted by scarcity.
It is protected by a line drawn through the middle of fullness.
Then God says:
It is not good for the man to be alone.
He brings every animal, every bird,
formed from the same ground as the man,
and the man names them.
Whatever he called each creature, that was its name.
The man exercises the delegated authority given in chapter one, naming,
as God named.
But among all the creatures,
no helper is found that corresponds to him.
God causes a deep sleep to fall.
He takes one from the man's side and closes the flesh.
He builds what He has taken into a woman and brings her to the man.
The man speaks, for the first time in Scripture, a human voice:
This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.
She shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man.
The Cup is shared.
It was never meant to be held alone.
The vessel that received breath now faces another vessel made from himself,
equal in substance, corresponding in form.
Therefore a man leaves his father and mother and joins to his wife,
and they become one flesh.
The man and his wife are both naked.
And they are not ashamed.
The Cup is transparent.
Everything is open.
Nothing is hidden.
There is no boundary between them that needs to be covered.
There is no gap between what they are and what they appear to be.
Two people stand in a garden with a boundary they have not yet crossed and a fullness they have not yet broken.
